summary.text: 吃 is a mouth-and-sound compound whose earliest supported sense is halting speech. It is also used for “eat,” but the history linking that use to the speech sense and to 喫 remains unsettled.

formation.text: The traditional analysis combines 口, contributing a speech-related meaning category, with 气 as the sound element. The modern right side is written like 乞; the precise graphic path between 气 and this form within 吃 is unresolved.

components.text: The left-hand 口 (“mouth”) contributes a speech-related meaning category in 吃. Its own pictographic history does not mean it depicts a scene here.

The right side is written like 乞, while the traditional analysis names 气 as the sound element. 乞 and 气 share an earlier graph in their separate history, but the specific graphic path within 吃 is not traced.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang-style Old Chinese, 吃 is reconstructed as *kɯd and 乞 as *kʰɯd(s). Their similarity supports a sound-series relationship, although the forms are not identical; modern Mandarin chī and qǐ differ.

history.text: The received Shuowen analysis records 从口气聲 and defines 吃 as difficult or halting speech. A transmitted Shiji passage also describes Han Fei as 口吃. These support the speech sense but do not establish the graph’s earliest physical form.

吃 and 喫 are both associated with eating, but accounts differ on the earliest spelling and the relationship between the graphs. Interchange, sound borrowing and simplification have been proposed; no sequence is established.

uncertainties.text: The earliest physical attestation of 吃 is unresolved. No inspected primary paleographic evidence establishes an oracle-bone or bronze form; reported Warring States ceramic and Western Han manuscript examples remain unverified leads.
The traditional analysis names 气, while the modern right side resembles 乞. The separate history of 乞 and 气 is described, but their dated graphic relationship within 吃 is not traced.
The earliest eating examples and the relationship among 吃, 喫, 齕 and related forms remain disputed. Dates of literary citations do not establish the dates of surviving physical witnesses.

senses.period: attested in the received Shiji text; physical witness dating unresolved
senses.text: The Shuowen entry defines 吃 as difficult or halting speech, and the transmitted Shiji passage describes Han Fei as 口吃. These attest the speech sense, not an eating sense.
吃 is recorded for eating or drinking and is associated with 喫. Its earliest spelling and relation to the speech sense remain unsettled.

senses.period: dating unresolved for 吃; Yuan-text examples are reported for 喫
senses.text: “Suffer” and “endure” are recorded glosses for 吃; Yuan-text examples are reported specifically for 喫. The chronology and semantic path to 吃 are not established here.
吃 is commonly used for “eat”; “drink” is also recorded. Its relation to the older speech sense remains unresolved.

limitations.text: The relationship between the eating use and the speech word is unresolved. The accounts do not determine whether it arose through semantic development, borrowing between graphs for similar-sounding words, or a separate graphic history, so no developmental chain is asserted.
Other recorded senses include absorbing, consuming, swallowing chess pieces and undergoing, but their chronology is insufficient to connect them reliably to the earliest attested sense.

overview.text: 吃 combines a mouth-related meaning element with a sound element. Its earliest supported meaning is halting speech; its familiar “eat” sense has a disputed history.

components.text: 口 contributes the speech-related meaning category in 吃.
The modern right side is written like 乞; the traditional analysis names 气. Their exact graphic connection within 吃 is unresolved.

takeaway.text: 吃 means “eat” today, but how that use relates to the older stammer sense and to 喫 remains unresolved.

relationships.text: 口 contributes the speech-related semantic category in the traditional phonosemantic analysis.
The traditional analysis names 气 as the sound element; the modern right side resembles 乞, and historical pronunciation comparison supports a sound-series relationship.
